Text: $TSLA Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, beating its own company-compiled analyst consensus of 461,974 by about 5.3%. The stock was up over 5% Friday. The comparison needs context. The 497,099 vehicles delivered in Q3 2025 were a pull-forward record, with buyers rushing the federal EV credit before it expired that September. Against that, a 2.1% YoY decline is not the headline. What caught my attention is the inventory line. Deliveries beat production by 22,141 vehicles, the second straight quarter Tesla sold more than it built, after Q2's 28,368 gap. The miss in the release was energy storage: 13.7 GWh deployed vs about 15.9 expected. Second-best quarter ever, up from 12.5 a year ago, but the Street wanted more. Full Q3 numbers come Oct 21.

Text: Is the current AI boom repeating the 2000 dot-com bubble again? $SPY $AAPL $TSLA $NVDA $MSFT There are genuine similarities such ad market leadership concentration, speculative enthusiasm. However, the key differences are far more significant. Valuations are nowhere near dot-com extremes, with the Nasdaq-100 trading around 26x forward earnings versus roughly 60x in 2000. Text: $TSLA Tesla Canada has stopped taking orders for the C$39,490 Model 3 Premium after strong demand used up its China import quota. The pause covers both the Rear-Wheel Drive and All-Wheel Drive versions. A banner on Tesla’s Canadian configurator says demand was so strong that the company burned through its share of the country’s quota for China-built EVs. Tesla expects orders to reopen in March 2027, as long as the government releases more quota. That timing lines up with Canada’s quota year for Chinese-made EVs, which starts on March 1. Nothing is official yet, so the date is best treated as Tesla’s estimate. If the planned 6.5% yearly increase goes ahead, next year’s pool could land at around 52,000 vehicles. The numbers also raise a question. That leaves more than 33,000 of the 33,397 spots unused. Canada hasn’t set per-brand limits and still issues permits first come, first served, so it’s unclear why Tesla’s allocation has already run out.

Author: TradeWithInsight
Text: $NFLX reports Tuesday after the close. $TSLA and $META report Wednesday after the close. When a company reports after the close, the stock reacts in after-hours trading and most of the move shows up as a gap at the next open. Options price that event in ahead of time. Implied volatility climbs into the report and drops right after it. That drop is called IV crush. It's why calls can lose value even when the stock goes up the next day. The move has to beat what the options already priced in.

Text: $TSLA It Was a "Hop," Not Sustained Flight The vehicle did not achieve sustained, controlled aerodynamic flight. Instead, the prototype used cold-gas thrusters derived from SpaceX technology to perform what amounted to a brief, high-energy jump—essentially an airborne stunt that lasted only a few seconds before the vehicle returned to the ground. Text: $TSLA The Physics of the "Empty Shell" Prominent figures, including Meta's Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun, quickly dismantled the physics behind the demonstration. • The Math: To lift a standard two-ton electric road car into the air would require an immense amount of thrust. Calculations show that even if 50% of the vehicle's total mass consisted of highly compressed air, the thrusters would deplete their entire supply in roughly 5 to 10 seconds. • The Trick: To make the car flip and land on its wheels during the demo, Tesla used an unmanned, stripped-down, lightweight shell of the vehicle. It lacked the massive batteries, passenger seats, interior components, and safety structures required for a road-legal car.

Author: kikiatwork
Text: $TSLA Total Lack of Practicality and Safety Even if a consumer version is delivered, the mechanics make it completely unusable for everyday transport: • Refill Times: The system relies on carbon-fiber pressure vessels holding air at an extreme 10,000 psi. Once those canisters empty after a single 3-second jump, refilling them using the onboard battery power could take anywhere from one to seven hours. • Extreme Danger: The deafening noise of 10,000 psi thrusters required spectators at the event to wear earplugs. On a public street, the downforce and high-pressure gas jets would blast debris like projectiles, risking severe injury to pedestrians and damaging surrounding property.

Author: kikiatwork
Text: $TSLA It is Not Street Legal or FAA Approved Tesla openly acknowledges on its website that the rocket thruster variant is not approved for use on public roads. Furthermore, aviation experts note that the vehicle does not meet the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) definition of an aircraft. Because it can neither legally drive on roads nor legally fly in regulated airspace, it functions purely as an expensive, invite-only toy for closed-course private tracks.

Author: kikiatwork
Text: $TSLA Distracting from a 9-Year Delay Many critics view the entire spectacle as a classic Silicon Valley distraction technique. Elon Musk first unveiled the Tesla Roadster prototype in 2017, taking hefty, non-refundable deposits from buyers who were promised a production car by 2020. Nearly a decade later, the production date has been pushed back yet again to 2028. The "flying" demonstration serves primarily to generate massive media engagement and placate frustrated deposit-holders, shifting the narrative from a severely delayed manufacturing schedule to a futuristic fantasy.
